Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers. 

And if the rest of the world is any precedent that would lead to a dramatic increase in overall bandwidth used. 

However, that would mean that mobile bandwidth usage would likely drop or stagnate with in home mobile usage.

"Right now, there don’t seem to be prospects of a negotiated settlement of the war in Ukraine. But the US is prepared to play whatever role we can in making that happen. It would be good for Russia and Ukraine, but so far, it’s proving elusive." - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio

In an interview with the Greek outlet Kathimerini, Rubio described the war in Ukraine as a "strategic stalemate" that can be overcome in only two ways: through negotiations or through escalation that goes beyond the original conflict.

Rubio said that, at present, there are no prospects for resolving the war through negotiations. According to him, Russia continues to insist on full control over Donbas, while for Ukraine "that condition is simply unacceptable."

"A diplomatic solution has eluded us, but we are prepared, if we can play a constructive role, to make it happen.

In the meantime, we watch with great concern as escalation could happen. Just yesterday, some ships were attacked in the Black Sea through a coordinated drone attack. We’re worried about a sabotage operation in a neighboring country that can spiral out of control.

And, obviously, there are clear indications that Russia will use the upcoming winter as something they want to use to destroy what remains of the electric grid in Ukraine and force them into capitulation.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has grown more effective in its ability to conduct long-range strikes deep into Russia.

So, we share the same concern. The whole world is going about this thing like something that could escalate and perhaps become a broader conflict. So, we stand prepared to facilitate and continue to explore any opportunity for a negotiated settlement," Rubio said.

🤡 “I want to thank President Putin”: Trump celebrates oil deal with Russia and brushes off Zelensky's criticism

Speaking to reporters outside the White House, the US president thanked Putin for promising to supply massive quantities of diesel fuel.

“This oil deal with Russia is a big deal. These are massive amounts of oil coming into our country. And it's diesel, which is exactly what we need. So, frankly, I want to thank President Putin,” Trump said.

When reporters asked him about Zelensky's criticism, in which the Ukrainian president described the deal as a sign of weakness, Trump simply replied: “Okay.”

Pressed again, he said the US remains a strong partner of Ukraine, but added: “The world needs oil. This is diesel, which the world needs. So we're very happy.”

Under the terms announced by Trump, Russia is expected to supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, another 500,000 tonnes in November, and 4 million tonnes over the following months.

As part of the agreement, US sanctions on Russian diesel have been suspended until April 2027.
